MainTech is an ambitious team of next-generation developers. Despite being 17 years old, we possess deep interdisciplinary expertise at the intersection of modern software engineering, systems analysis, and applied physics.

Behind us are successful participations in prestigious hackathons and the development of full-cycle technological projects (ranging from high-performance backend architectures to interactive 3D interfaces).
summary:
LunarWindow — Lunar Landing Site Navigator

LunarWindow is a mission-planning tool that answers a critical question for lunar landers: not just where to land, but when. For any site on the Moon and any date, it computes whether the Sun is available for power and whether Earth is above the horizon for direct communication. It also counts down the hours to sunset and Earthset, and shows how a schedule slip changes mission feasibility.

The engine runs on real flight-grade data: JPL DE440 ephemerides and the lunar orientation model in the MOON_ME frame, with libration included. It treats the Sun as a finite, limb-darkened disk and accounts for lunar curvature (R = 1737.4 km). Because the Moon has no atmosphere, there is no refraction to correct for. Sunrise and sunset times are resolved to within half a second. A scenario engine compares a baseline mission with a delayed or relocated one and returns a **GO / CAUTION / NO-GO** verdict against battery and communication constraints.

The project combines a FastAPI backend with an interactive 3D web experience built with Three.js and custom Blender assets. It covers 14 catalogued sites, including the Apollo landings, Artemis III candidate regions, CLPS and international missions. Its architecture is ready for LRO LOLA terrain horizon profiles.

details:
What it does and how it works
LunarWindow tells mission planners where and when a lander can operate on the Moon. The user picks a landing site and a date, and the backend computes the Sun's and Earth's position above the local horizon from JPL DE440 ephemerides, in the MOON_ME frame and including libration. From that it calculates:

  • solar power: the visible fraction of a limb-darkened solar disk, giving irradiance in W/m²;
  • direct-to-Earth communication windows;
  • countdowns to sunset and Earthset, with event times precise to 0.5 s.

A scenario engine compares a baseline mission with a delayed or relocated one and returns a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict.

Benefits
It replaces rough estimates with physics-based answers in seconds. Teams can see how a schedule slip affects power and communication before it becomes a mission risk. This matters most at the lunar south pole, where the Sun stays within 1.5° of the horizon.

Intended impact
Faster, safer landing-site and launch-window decisions for Artemis-era and commercial (CLPS) missions. It also makes lunar mission constraints understandable to students and the public.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy, JPL DE440 kernels.
  • Frontend: JavaScript, React, Vite, Three.js (with post-processing), GSAP, Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D assets: Blender.
  • Hosting: Vercel.

Creative approach
Real flight-grade physics wrapped in a cinematic, scroll-driven 3D presentation. Complex orbital mechanics becomes a simple, interactive story: pick a site, pick a date, see the verdict.

Factors we considered

  • Lunar curvature (R = 1737.4 km).
  • No atmosphere, so no refraction.
  • The Sun's finite size and limb darkening.
  • Earth libration (±8°).
  • Battery autonomy and communication blackout limits.
  • Honest limitations: terrain horizons are currently spherical, and the API is ready for LRO LOLA profiles.
